source_text: Attende igitur, quid disputatio tota confecerit. Si gratia Christi et Adae culpa in diversis effectibus aequaliter censerentur, ut vel numero operationum pares essent, quae operationum genere dissidebant, docendum erat tantis profuisse gratiam, quantis culpa nocuisset, ut appensionis illius, qua trutinabantur, aequitas et momenta constarent. Subvenire ergo debuit etiam illis omnino locis illisque partibus medicina, quibus insederat aegritudo, id est si aliquid in motibus genitalium, in sensibus coeuntium, in obscaenitate membrorum, in infelicitate nascentium antiquum crimen effecerat, immutatione horum, quae diximus, remedia contulisset; alioquin grande testimonium imbecillae artis nihilque profuturae nec locum aegritudinis invenisse et languentibus eversisque naturalibus inertia fomenta voluntatibus admovisse.
pass_a_gloss: Attend therefore what the whole disputation has brought about. If the grace of Christ and Adam's fault were estimated equally in diverse effects, so that they would be equal even by the number of operations, which disagreed by the kind of operations, it would have to be taught that grace helped as many as fault had harmed, so that the equity and moments of that weighing by which they were being trutinated would stand. Help therefore ought to have come even to those places altogether and those parts with medicine, in which the sickness had sat, that is if an ancient crime had effected anything in the motions of the genitals, in the senses of those coupling, in the obscenity of the members, in the unhappiness of those being born, it would have conferred remedies by a change of these things which we have said; otherwise a great testimony of a weak art and about to profit nothing both not to have found the place of sickness and to have applied inert fomentations to languishing and overturned natural wills.

pass_b_english: Consider, then, what the whole argument has established. If Christ’s grace and Adam’s fault were judged equal in their opposite effects—equal at least in the number of their operations, though differing in kind—it would have to be shown that grace benefited as many as the fault harmed, so that the balance and weight of the scale in which they were weighed remained fair. The medicine should therefore have helped in precisely the places and parts where the disease had settled. If the ancient crime had done anything to genital movements, the sensations of those coupling, the shamefulness of bodily parts, or the misery of newborn children, grace should have brought remedies by changing those things. Otherwise, it would be striking evidence of a feeble and useless medical art that it failed even to find the disease’s location, and, while the natural functions lay sick and ruined, applied ineffective soothing treatments to people’s wills.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
